questions.q: A researcher finishes their daily experiment, signs their work, and realizes that the bottom half of their official, bound laboratory notebook page is completely empty. To strictly adhere to legal and intellectual property guidelines, how must the researcher handle this blank space?
options: Leave the space completely blank so they can add tomorrow's data to the same page to save paper.
Use scissors to cut out the blank half of the page to reduce the physical weight of the notebook.
Draw a single, solid diagonal line through the blank space, and sign and date across the line.
Cover the blank space entirely with white-out correction fluid so nothing can be written there.
questions.explain:
A laboratory notebook is a legally binding document that can be subpoenaed in court to prove patent priority (who invented what first) or regulatory compliance. 

Blank spaces create an opportunity for someone to retroactively and fraudulently add data days or months later. To secure the chronological integrity of the record, researchers must draw a **single diagonal strike-through line** across any significant empty space, accompanied by their **signature (or initials) and the date**, proving the page was sealed exactly when the work was finished.

questions.q: According to universal Good Documentation Practices (GDP), why is the use of pencils, erasable pens, or water-soluble markers strictly prohibited when recording raw data in an official laboratory notebook?
options: Pencil graphite physically interferes with the highly sensitive electromagnetic sensors inside analytical balances.
Only data recorded in indelible, permanent ink guarantees that the record cannot be covertly erased, altered, or forged after the initial entry.
Erasable inks and graphite undergo rapid, explosive chemical reactions when exposed to standard autoclaving temperatures.
Standard FDA optical scanning software is electronically programmed to ignore non-ink written text.
questions.explain:
Good Documentation Practices (GDP) mandate that all scientific and manufacturing records must be permanent and legible. 

The strict requirement for **indelible, permanent ink (usually blue or black)** prevents data falsification. If a pencil is used, a technician could secretly erase failing results and rewrite passing ones, destroying the legal and scientific integrity of the data. Ink ensures that any mistakes made must be formally crossed out, leaving the original data visible and accountable.
